title-group.article-title: Removal of Sr (II) from aqueous solutions by adsorption using amberlite XAD-7 resin impregnated with TOPO extractant

abstract.p: This research investigation deals with efficiently removing strontium ions from aqueous solutions, a problem with significant environmental and health implications due to radioactive contamination. The performance and potential of Amberlite XAD-7 resin impregnated with TOPO extractant was evaluated to remove strontium ions from aqueous solutions. The influence of main operating conditions such as the initial pH, initial concentration of strontium in the solution, contact time, impregnation ratio, and adsorbent dosage, was evaluated. The adsorbents were characterized using SEM and FTIR analyses both before and after impregnation, as well as after the adsorption process. The study of the effect of contact time on the adsorption process was carried out in order to achieve the adsorption equilibrium time and determine the appropriate kinetic model. The experimental results showed that the adsorption process reaches equilibrium within 240 min, and the pseudo-second-order kinetic model is very suitable to describe this adsorption process (R2 > 0.99). Adsorption equilibrium modeling showed that the Langmuir isotherm model can well describe the equilibrium behavior of strontium adsorption by Amberlite XAD-7 resin impregnated with TOPO extractant (R2 > 0.99). The maximum uptake predicted by the Langmuir model for strontium adsorption using the TOPO impregnated Amberlite XAD-7 was 65.79 mg/g.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Strontium-90 (Sr-90) is a highly radioactive isotope generated as a byproduct of uranium fission, posing significant risks to human health and the environment1. With a physical half-life of approximately 29 years and a biological half-life of about 49 years, Sr-90’s persistence in the environment raises substantial concerns, particularly following nuclear accidents or incidents involving the release of nuclear waste2. Its propensity to dissolve in water means that it can easily migrate into surface water systems, leading to contamination that affects both ecosystems and human populations. The health implications of Sr-90 exposure are severe; once ingested, it behaves similarly to calcium and preferentially accumulates in bones and teeth3. This accumulation can lead to various forms of cancer, including bone cancer and leukemia, due to the high-energy beta radiation emitted during its decay4. The widespread dissemination of Sr-90 into the environment has been linked to historical nuclear testing and accidents, such as those at Chernobyl and Fukushima, further complicating efforts to manage its presence in contaminated sites5. Consequently, to mitigate the risks associated with Sr-90, effective management strategies are essential6.

Traditional chemical methods for removing strontium, other metal ions, and pollutants from industrial wastewater include precipitation7, electrochemical treatment8, distillation9,10, filtration11, ion exchange12, reverse osmosis13, membrane technologies14–16, solvent extraction17,18, and adsorption2,19–31, have been used to remove strontium from industrial wastewater. Among these methods, solvent extraction is favored in industrial applications due to its efficiency and selectivity in separating heavy metals32–35.

Extractants such as Tributyl Phosphate (TBP) and Tri-n-octylphosphine Oxide (TOPO) have proven effective in this regard36–38. In particular, the use of TOPO for strontium extraction presents a promising avenue for research39–41. By impregnating TOPO onto solid resin adsorbents like Amberlite XAD-7, researchers can leverage both the extractant’s solubility and the resin’s adsorption capabilities to enhance strontium removal from aqueous solutions. This dual-action approach not only improves extraction efficiency but also offers a more sustainable method for managing radioactive waste.

Ion exchange resins have gained significant attention for their effectiveness in removing heavy metals such as strontium. Ease of handling, high efficiency, and ability to be regenerated make them a preferred method in various applications42. Among these, Amberlite XAD-7 resin has demonstrated promising capabilities in adsorbing strontium ions2. To further enhance the adsorption capacity and selectivity of Amberlite XAD-7 for strontium, this study explores the impregnation of TOPO onto the resin. This approach, utilizing solvent impregnated resins (SIR), represents a novel method aimed at increasing strontium adsorption efficiency. TOPO is a neutral phosphorus-containing organic ligand known for its ability to coordinate into stable complexes with strontium ions, consequently improving the resin’s adsorption characteristics43. Previous studies have indicated that incorporating extractants can significantly enhance the adsorption characteristics of resins44–48. The implementation of SIRs yields multiple significant improvements over traditional extraction methods, including enhanced selectivity of extractants, efficient recovery of adsorbed materials during desorption, and a diverse range of extractants available for various applications. The primary objective of this research is to investigate the adsorption potential of TOPO impregnated Amberlite XAD-7 for the removal of strontium from waste waters. Additionally, the study aims to evaluate how the impregnation process affects the overall adsorption capacity of the adsorbent.

This study has aimed to evaluate the adsorption capacity of TOPO impregnated Amberlite XAD-7 resin for adsorbing strontium. Key factors influencing removal efficiency, including initial solution pH, contact time, adsorbent dosage, initial concentration of Sr (II), and degree of impregnation, have been systematically examined. Additionally, the equilibrium and kinetics of the strontium sorption process have also been investigated.

sec.title: Reagents
sec.p: Amberlite XAD-7 resins (20–50 mesh, analytical grade) and Trioctyl phosphine oxide (TOPO, purity > 98%) purchased from Sigma-Aldridge. All chemical reagents, including Strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, Toluene (C6H5CH3), Nitric acid (HNO3), and Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) were of analytical grade and supplied by Merck (Darmstadt, Germany).

sec.title: Impregnation procedure
sec.p: First, Amberlite XAD-7 was impregnated with TOPO extractant before performing experiments. The amount of 30 g of resin was washed three times with deionized water to eliminate impurities, and then it was filtered and dried for a whole day at 25 °C. Ten grams of the prepared dry resins were contacted at room temperature with 30 and 60 g of TOPO in 0.5 M toluene solution for 24 h to prepare two SIRs with two degrees of impregnation, respectively. The resin beads, after impregnation, were separated from the organic phase and rinsed several times with 2 M nitric acid. They were subsequently washed with deionized water, dried in an oven at 50 °C for 12 h, and stored for later use.

sec.title: Sorption method
sec.p: To conduct strontium ion adsorption experiments using Amberlite XAD-7 resin and prepared SIRs, determined amounts of these adsorbents were added into a series of 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks, each containing 100 mL of strontium nitrate solution at specified concentrations. A 0.1 M sodium hydroxide solution and a 0.1 M nitric acid solution were used to adjust the pH. The flasks were then placed in an incubator shaker and agitated at 150 rpm for a set duration at room temperature. In certain time intervals, the solution was sampled and the metal ion concentrations in these samples were measured using inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) with a PerkinElmer Optima 7300 DV instrument (USA). All experiments were performed in duplicate, and the average values were reported to minimize errors.

sec.title: Characterization
sec.p: Figure 1 displays the Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) spectra of the blank Amberlite XAD-7 resin, as well as the TOPO-impregnated XAD-7 both before and after the adsorption process. The spectra cover the range from 500 to 4000 cm− 1. The broad band in the range of 3700 cm- 1 to 3100 cm- 1 is related to the stretching vibration of hydroxyl, indicating the presence of some free water adsorbed from the air by the Amberlite XAD-7 resin. The peaks seen at 2990 and 2921 cm-1 belong to the stretching vibrations of the -CH3 and -CH2 groups resulting from the impregnation of TOPO molecules on the XAD-7 resin. The stretches at 1725 cm- 1 are related to the C = O, and 1262 cm- 1 corresponds to the C-O stretching in the ester. The stretching vibration of the P = O bond appears as a peak at 1360 and 1141 cm- 1, and the peak of 942 cm- 1 is related to the stretching vibration of P-O-H, which indicates the successful impregnation of the resin (Fig. 1(b)). The FTIR spectrum after Sr (II) adsorption (Fig. 1)c() shows that the intensity of the characteristic peaks for the TOPO impregnated Amberlite resin at 2990, 1141, and 942 cm[- [1 decreases, indicating the role of alkyl, and phosphoryl and phosphonyl functional groups in the adsorption process.

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) analysis was conducted to examine the surface morphology of the resin and its alterations resulting from impregnation and subsequent strontium adsorption. Based on Fig. 2, Dowex 50 W-X8 has a symmetrical and dense surface with small pores (Fig. 2a), while its surface after impregnation has become rougher and the resin pores have also opened up (Fig. 2b). Figure 2b illustrates that the resin surface has been modified with TOPO, and the solvent has nearly filled all the pores. After the adsorption of Sr ions by the Amberlite XAD-7 impregnated with TOPO, the surface becomes denser and fine pores are not visible on the resin surface, as shown in Fig. 2c. Strontium ions appear to be sitting as bright spots on the surface of the impregnated resin.

SEM images of Amberlite XAD-7 resin before a and after b impregnation, and after strontium adsorption c.

sec.title: Effect of pH
sec.p: Influence of pH on the uptake of strontium ions by Amberlite XAD-7 resin, and Amberlite-TOPO SIRs at two different ratios are shown in Fig. 3. As shown in this figure, at lower pHs the adsorption value is low. With increasing the pH, the adsorption capacity increases and reaches to a maximum value at pH 6. With a further increase in pH, the amount of adsorption decreases again. This phenomenon is due to the competition of H+ cations with Sr2+ cations to occupy the available exchange sites, which at low pH has a high concentration of H+ cations and therefore, the amount of the adsorption is low. The adsorption was not examined under alkaline pH conditions because of the potential precipitation of strontium50.

caption.p: Effect of pH on strontium adsorption. (Co: 50 mg/L, Adsorbent dosage: 0.75 g/L, contact time: 24 h).

sec.p: TOPO contains an oxygen ion in the oxygen-phosphorus bond, which can be seen in the FTIR graph with a peak at 1141 cm- 1 corresponding to the P = O stretching vibration (Fig. 1). Divalent strontium ions (Sr2+) can potentially form complexes with oxygens present in two TOPO molecules (Fig. 4(b)). However, monovalent Sr(OH)+ ions require only one ،TOPO molecule to form the complex. Therefore, complexing of monovalent ions with TOPO is easier than that of divalent ions. Given that at higher pHs, according to solution chemistry, the presence of monovalent ions is greater than that of divalent ions and the higher accessibility of adsorption sites for monovalent ions compared to divalent ions51, the adsorption capacity increases. These evidences suggest that the main adsorption mechanism in the adsorption of Sr(II) ions by Amberlite-TOPO SIR is ion exchange by the resin and complex formation by the extractant. Other researchers have also reached similar results for the metal ions, chromium and lanthanum52,53.

caption.p: The TOPO chemical structure (a) and simple representation for the strontium ions complexing with TOPO.

sec.title: Effect of impregnation ratio
sec.p: To evaluate how the resin impregnation ratio affects strontium adsorption, three experimental series were conducted: without impregnation, with an impregnation ratio of 0.386 g/g SIR, and with 0.473 g/g SIR, across a pH range of 2–7. As shown in Fig. 3, adsorption capacity rises as impregnation is applied and also with increasing its ratio over the entire pH range studied. This observation suggests that in the impregnated resin, both the support (Amberlite XAD-7) and the solvent (TOPO) participate in strontium adsorption, resulting in increased adsorption capacity. As can be seen in Fig. 3, at the optimum pH of 6, the adsorption rate increased from 33.65 to 48.23 mg/g with an increase in the impregnation ratio from 0.386 to 0.473 g/g SIR.

sec.title: Effect of contact time
sec.p: The adsorption of strontium ions was studied using three adsorbents: Amberlite XAD-7 and Amberlite-TOPO SIRs with impregnation ratios of 0.386 and 0.473 g/g SIR, at different time intervals. Dynamic adsorption experiments showed that the process is relatively rapid initially, with about 70% of the total adsorption occurring within the first 60 min (Fig. 5). Subsequently, the adsorption rate decreased and reached equilibrium in approximately 240 min.

caption.p: The Effect of contact time on strontium adsorption. (pH: 6, Co: 50 mg/L, Adsorbent dosage: 0.75 g/L).

sec.title: Effect of adsorbent dosage
sec.p: The effect of adsorbent dosage on the adsorption of strontium by the Amberlite XAD-7 resin was studied in the range of 0.25 to 2 g/L, as shown in Fig. 6. It is clear that removal percentage increased by increasing the dosage of the adsorbent, owing to the higher availability of sites for metal ion adsorption. As the adsorbent dosage increases, the adsorption amount per unit weight of adsorbent decreases. Therefore, 0.75 g adsorbent / 1 litter of solution, was considered as an optimum dosage for all the adsorption experiments.

caption.p: Effect of adsorbent (non-impregnated) dosage on adsorption of strontium. (pH: 6, Co: 50 mg/L).

sec.title: Effect of initial solution concentration
sec.p: The effect of the initial solution concentration on adsorption capacity is illustrated in Fig. 7 for both impregnated and non-impregnated adsorbents. As shown, strontium adsorption increases sharply with rising initial concentration until it approaches a plateau. The reason for this is that the initial concentration acts as the driving force of adsorption and increases the amount of adsorption. But at higher concentrations, owing to the saturation of the adsorption sites, there is no improvement in the adsorption amount.

caption.p: Effect of initial concentration on strontium adsorption. (pH: 6, Adsorbent dosage: 0.75 g/L).

sec.title: Kinetic study

caption.p: Kinetics of strontium adsorption onto impregnated and nonimpregnated Amberlite XAD-7 (pH: 6, Co: 50 mg/L, Adsorbent dosage: 0.75 g/L).

sec.title: Adsorption isotherms
sec.p: To design an adsorption system for metal ion separation, selecting an appropriate isotherm model to describe equilibrium data is essential. In this study, the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models were examined to fit the equilibrium results.

caption.p: Adsorption isotherms of Sr2+ ion adsorbed onto impregnated and non-impregnated Amberlite XAD-7 (pH: 6, Adsorbent dosage: 0.75 g/L).

sec.p: The maximum adsorption capacity obtained for this impregnated resin was compared with reported values for strontium adsorption by similar adsorbents, as summarized in Table 3. According to the data presented, the adsorbents evaluated in this study exhibit notably high maximum adsorption capacities. Therefore, the impregnated resin possesses sufficient adsorption performance to be considered a strong candidate for practical implementation in industrial strontium-removal applications.

caption.p: A comparison of various adsorbents in terms of their ability to adsorb strontium.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In the present research, the adsorption of strontium on Amberlite XAD-7 impregnated with TOPO was investigated. The effects of independent process variables including pH, contact time, adsorbent dosage, and initial strontium concentration on the adsorption amount were investigated. The findings indicated that the impregnation of Amberlite XAD-7 with TOPO markedly enhances the adsorption capacity of the adsorbent. Moreover, the adsorption kinetics of strontium on this adsorbent follows the pseudo-second-order model. The adsorption process reached equilibrium after about 240 min of contact. The Langmuir equation provides a good fit to the experimental data. From the results of the Langmuir model, the maximum adsorption amount of strontium on Amberlite XAD-7 impregnated with TOPO was 65.79 mg/g. This approach shows potential for application in environmental and industrial settings, although considerations regarding cost and scalability should be further evaluated.
